steps.prompt: One bell rings every $12$ minutes and another every $18$ minutes. They ring together at noon. When do they next ring together?

cards.title: Greatest common divisor, least common multiple
cards.body: Write both numbers as primes. The GCD takes each shared prime to the SMALLER power; the LCM takes every prime to the LARGER power. For $84 = 2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 7$ and $120 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$: $\gcd = 2^2 \cdot 3 = 12$ and $\text{lcm} = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 5 \cdot 7 = 840$.

cards.title: Worked example: the bells
cards.problem: Bells ring every $12$ and $18$ minutes and ring together at noon. How many minutes until they ring together again?

steps.text: $12 = 2^2 \cdot 3$ and $18 = 2 \cdot 3^2$. Together again after a common multiple of both.
The first time is the LCM: $2^2 \cdot 3^2 = 36$ minutes, at $12{:}36$.

cards.title: The product rule
cards.body: For any two positive whole numbers, $\gcd(a, b) \times \text{lcm}(a, b) = a \times b$. So if you know three of the four numbers, you know the fourth. Numbers with $\gcd = 1$ are called relatively prime; their LCM is just their product.

cards.title: Worked example: the missing number
cards.problem: Two numbers have GCD $6$ and LCM $180$. One of them is $36$. What is the other?

steps.text: GCD $\times$ LCM $= 6 \times 180 = 1080$, which is the product of the two numbers.

cards.title: The common trap: multiplying instead of the LCM
cards.body: The product $12 \times 18 = 216$ is A common multiple, but not the LEAST unless the GCD is $1$. Decide which you need: "together again" or "fits into both evenly" is an LCM; "largest equal pieces" or "largest square tiles" is a GCD.

prompts: How do you decide whether a word problem wants the GCD or the LCM?
